slides.title: Market Demand
slides.text:
Market Demand
Law of Demand: Other things being the same, the quantity demanded of a good falls when its price increases.
Market Demand Curve: Shows the amount of a good that will be purchased at alternative prices, holding other factors constant.
The demand curve is downward sloping.

bullets.text: Law of Demand: Other things being the same, the quantity demanded of a good falls when its price increases.
Market Demand Curve: Shows the amount of a good that will be purchased at alternative prices, holding other factors constant.
The demand curve is downward sloping.

slides.visual_text: Next to the Law of Demand and Market Demand Curve bullets, a graph with Price on the vertical axis and Quantity on the horizontal axis shows a straight line D sloping downward from left to right.

slides.title: The Demand Function
slides.text: The Demand Function
slides.visual_text: The Demand Function: a general equation representing the demand curve, Qxd = f(Px, Py, M, H). Qxd = quantity demand of good X. Px = price of good X. Py = price of a related good Y: substitute good, complement good. M = income: normal good, inferior good. H = any other variable affecting demand.

slides.title: Question
slides.text: Question
slides.visual_text: Question. The demand for good X is given by: Qxd = 140 - 5Px + 4Py - 6Pz + 0.01M. Research shows that Py = ₹50, Pz = ₹40, and average income M = ₹30,000. Is Y a substitute or complement for X? Is Z a substitute or complement for X? Is X a normal good or an inferior good? Determine the inverse demand function for X. Graph it. (Do it at home!) How many units of X will be purchased when Px = ₹ 40? The slide gives no answers.

slides.title: Consumer Surplus
slides.text:
Consumer Surplus
The value consumers get from a good but do not have to pay for
Consumer surplus isn't just a triangle on a graph - it's what marketers try to capture
Value pricing → charging closer to what each customer is willing to pay
Price discrimination → segmenting customers to capture surplus from different groups at different prices

slides.title: Consumer Surplus: The Discrete Case
slides.text: Consumer Surplus: The Discrete Case
slides.visual_text: Graph titled Consumer Surplus: The Discrete Case. Price axis marked 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Quantity axis marked 1 to 5. A straight demand line D runs from a price of 10 down to a quantity of 5. Green bars under the line: the first unit up to 8, the second up to 6, the third up to 4. A red rectangle at a price of 2 covers quantities 0 to 4 (the amount paid). Callout: Consumer Surplus: The value received but not paid for. Consumer surplus = (8-2) + (6-2) + (4-2) = $12.

slides.title: Consumer Surplus: The Continuous Case
slides.text: Consumer Surplus: The Continuous Case
slides.visual_text: Graph titled Consumer Surplus: The Continuous Case. Price $ axis marked 2 to 10; Quantity axis marked 1 to 5. Demand line D from a price of 10 down to a quantity of 5. The green area under D down to a price of 2, out to 4 units, is the consumer surplus; the red rectangle below a price of 2, from 0 to 4 units, is spending. Callouts: Value of 4 units = $24 (the whole area under D up to 4 units). Expenditure on 4 units = $2 x 4 = $8. Consumer Surplus = $24 - $8 = $16.

slides.title: Market Supply Curve
slides.text:
Market Supply Curve
The supply curve shows the amount of a good that will be produced at alternative prices.
Law of Supply
The supply curve is upward sloping showing that quantity supplied increases as prices increase, other things remaining the same.

slides.title: The Supply Function
slides.text: The Supply Function
slides.visual_text: The Supply Function: an equation representing the supply curve, Qxs = f(Px, Pr, W, H). Qxs = quantity supplied of good X. Px = price of good X. Pr = price of a production substitute. W = price of inputs (e.g., wages). H = other variable affecting supply.

slides.title: Question
slides.text: Question
slides.visual_text: Question. The supply function for product X is given by: Qxs = 40 + 5Px - 3Pz, where Pz is the price of a key input. How much of X is produced when Px = ₹ 100 and Pz = ₹ 30? How much of X is produced when Px = ₹ 20 and Pz = ₹ 30? Suppose Pz = ₹ 30. Determine the (reduced) supply function and the inverse supply function for X. Graph the inverse supply function. (Do it at home!) The slide gives no answers.

slides.title: Producer Surplus
slides.text:
Producer Surplus
The amount producers receive in excess of the amount necessary to induce them to produce the good.

bullets.text: The amount producers receive in excess of the amount necessary to induce them to produce the good.

slides.visual_text: Next to the definition, a graph with an upward sloping supply curve S0. A dashed line marks price P* and quantity Q*. The green triangle between the price line P* and the supply curve, from zero out to Q*, is the producer surplus.

slides.text: Market Equilibrium
slides.visual_text: Text: The Price (P) that balances supply and demand: Qxs = Qxd; No shortage or surplus. Steady-state. Picture: a black balance scale with two pans level.

slides.title: Price Restrictions
slides.text:
Price Restrictions
Price Ceilings
The maximum legal price that can be charged.
Examples: National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) fixing prices of stents and other price saving drugs, Price caps on surge pricing for Uber / Ola
Price Floors
The minimum legal price that can be charged.
Examples:
Minimum wage.
Agricultural price supports.

slides.title: Impact of a Price Ceiling
slides.text: Impact of a Price Ceiling
slides.visual_text: Graph titled Impact of a Price Ceiling. Demand D and supply S cross at P* and Q*. A red horizontal line P Ceiling sits below P*. At the ceiling, the supply curve gives Qs and the demand curve gives Qd, with Qs to the left of Q* and Qd to the right; the gap between them is labelled Shortage. A purple dashed line goes up from Qs to the demand curve and across to a higher price PF on the price axis, above P*.

slides.title: Full Economic Price
slides.text: Full Economic Price
slides.visual_text: Full Economic Price: The dollar amount paid to a firm under a price ceiling, plus the nonpecuniary price. Pf = Pc + (Pf - Pc). Pf = full economic price. Pc = price ceiling. Pf - Pc = nonpecuniary price.

slides.title: Impact of a Price Floor
slides.text: Impact of a Price Floor
slides.visual_text: Graph titled Impact of a Price Floor. Demand D and supply S cross at P* and Q*. A red horizontal line PF sits above P*. At PF, the demand curve gives Qd (left of Q*) and the supply curve gives QS (right of Q*); the gap between them is labelled Surplus.

slides.title: Big Picture Analysis: PC Market
slides.text:
Big Picture Analysis: PC Market
Equilibrium price of PCs will fall, and equilibrium quantity of computers sold will increase.
Action Plan:
inventories?
Existing stock built with expensive components → losing value as market price falls
Sell down inventory faster rather than hold
Time new production to align with cheaper components
human resources?
Equilibrium quantity ↑ → industry-wide demand for PCs growing. Staff up production to capture higher volume?
marketing?
Lead with price cuts to match falling market price?
Or protect margin — bundle features/software instead of cutting price?
do I need quantitative estimates?
Direction alone (price ↓, quantity ↑) isn't enough to act on
How much to cut price — 3%? 8%?
How much more to order? Needs: demand elasticity, size of cost shift, competitor pass-through

slides.title: Big Picture Analysis: Software Market
slides.text:
Big Picture Analysis: Software Market
Software prices are likely to rise, and more software will be sold.
Use this to organize an action plan.
inventories?
Ramp up cloud infrastructure ahead of the expected demand surge, rather than scrambling reactively
human resources?
Rising quantity sold → more customers needing onboarding, support, updates
Staff up customer support and sales before the PC price drop fully plays out, not after demand has already spiked
marketing?
Since software price is expected to rise, this is a moment to lean into value-based messaging rather than discounting
Time a product launch or feature release to coincide with the PC upgrade cycle this event will trigger → new PC buyers are a captive audience for new software
do I need quantitative estimates?
Need: cross-price elasticity between PCs and software (how strongly linked are the two demands?), and how much of the PC price drop actually reaches consumers vs. gets absorbed by PC makers' margins

organize an action plan (needed changes in production, inventories, raw materials, human resources, marketing plans, etc.).
